note: As of 07:02 SGT Thu 19 Nov, pre-Asia-open (SGX/HKEX not yet trading). All items below are from the Wed 18 Nov US/global session or later except the Mon 16 Nov Singapore-REIT item, which is retained for its direct relevance to the SGX REIT sleeve.

items.headline: Precious-metals miners crushed far harder than bullion -- GDX -6.94%, SILJ -5.85%, SLVP -6.52% vs GLD -2.48%, SLV -4.69%
items.summary: Gold broke below $3,800 (14-month low) and silver fell toward $46 as Fed hike odds for Dec 9 firmed to ~95-98% and the dollar pushed to roughly a 19-month high, driving a broad precious-metals selloff. Miners (GDX, SILJ, SLVP, NEM, PAAS, AG, HL) fell 1.5-3x harder than the metals themselves -- consistent with operating leverage (fixed mining costs mean every dollar move in the metal swings profit, and therefore the equity, by a larger percentage) rather than any mining-specific scandal; no CME margin-requirement hike was identified as a distinct trigger for the day.
items.actionable: This was a macro/leverage event (hawkish Fed + strong dollar), not an idiosyncratic miner-specific risk -- but that same operating leverage means GDX/SILJ/SLVP will keep amplifying whatever bullion does next, so stress-test margin buffers on the levered silver book against further dollar strength into the Dec 9 FOMC rather than against a miner-specific headline risk.

items.headline: MP Materials +8%, USA Rare Earth +7% on US-China rare-earth-talks optimism; Needham reinstates MP at Buy, $48 PT
items.summary: Rare-earth equities jumped as traders positioned for rare-earth supply-chain discussion at the Trump-Xi-Putin APEC summit in Shenzhen, with MP Materials up roughly 8% and USA Rare Earth up ~7%. Separately, Needham analyst James Ricchiuti reinstated MP coverage with a Buy rating and $48 price target (~38% upside), citing progress at Mountain Pass including expanded heavy-rare-earth separation capacity and MP's position as an emerging vertically-integrated magnet supplier with GM/Apple offtake and US government backing.
items.actionable: The pop is sentiment/headline-driven (summit anticipation plus a single fresh analyst call) rather than new fundamental data, so it reinforces the long-term DoD/magnet thesis without confirming a re-rating -- a reasonable watchlist add on confirmation of constructive Shenzhen headlines, not a chase at the open.

items.headline: Lynas rebounds 2.83% to A$12.37 after Tuesday's 8.2% plunge -- broad commodity-rout bounce, not company-specific
items.summary: Lynas shares recovered Wednesday after copper, iron ore, lithium, uranium and rare-earth names were all sold heavily Tuesday in an indiscriminate commodities rout; there was no new Lynas-specific catalyst behind either the Tuesday drop or Wednesday's bounce. The stock remains roughly 45% below its A$22.37 52-week high, well under the ~A$16.35 average analyst price target, even after a quarterly update showing sales revenue +55% YoY and a record average selling price of A$102.1/kg.
items.actionable: This reads as beta/mean-reversion after an indiscriminate selloff rather than thesis confirmation -- the underlying operating metrics (record ASP, strong revenue growth) are genuinely positive, but don't mistake Wednesday's bounce for a resolved uptrend given the stock is still far below both its highs and consensus targets.

items.headline: FOMC minutes: 'almost all' participants see further hikes likely appropriate; 10-2 vote masked a closer internal debate
items.summary: The October FOMC minutes showed the committee held rates at 3.75-4.00% by a 10-2 vote (Cook and Hammack dissenting in favor of a 25bp hike), but revealed 'some participants' beyond the two dissenters favored hiking at that meeting, and a couple flagged a move larger than 25bp as worth considering in December. The hawkish tone pushed the dollar to roughly a 19-month high and firmed Dec 9 hike odds to ~95-98%, with gold and Bitcoin each falling 3%+ and oil down about 3% in the reaction.
items.actionable: No dovish surprise emerged -- the minutes confirm rather than reverse the hawkish repricing that is the single biggest threat to the levered silver/miners book, so the working assumption should remain continued dollar strength and rate pressure into the Dec 9 decision.

items.headline: Trump-Xi-Putin hold unprecedented trilateral summit at APEC Shenzhen -- trade, chip export controls and rare earths on the agenda
items.summary: Trump arrived in Shenzhen for a first-ever three-way summit with Xi and Putin, with the agenda spanning AI/semiconductor export controls, rare-earth supply chains, Ukraine and Iran alongside trade. Trump claimed US rare-earth production would match China's within a year, referencing the prior APEC-summit truce under which China paused export controls in exchange for tariff relief and resumed US soybean/fentanyl-precursor cooperation.
items.actionable: No concrete new agreement has been confirmed yet -- watch the next 24-48 hours for a joint statement specifically on rare-earth export controls or chip licensing, which could move the HK-tech and rare-earth sleeves sharply in either direction.

items.headline: Oil tumbles as API shows 5.28mn-barrel US crude build; IEA's Q4 surplus call weighs
items.summary: WTI and Brent both fell sharply (WTI toward $83-84, Brent toward $91-92) after the American Petroleum Institute reported a 5.28-million-barrel US crude inventory build for the week ended Nov 13, reinforcing the IEA's Nov 13 Oil Market Report call that global supply should return to surplus in Q4 as Middle East exports recover faster than demand. Ongoing US-Iran friction and Strait of Hormuz shipping risk limited, but did not reverse, the decline.
items.actionable: No direct portfolio holding here, but the inventory-build/surplus story is a genuine disinflationary data point that modestly cuts against the hawkish-Fed narrative -- a secondary input for the cash-pile rate view, not yet enough to move Dec-hike pricing.

items.headline: Bitcoin breaks below its 200-week moving average -- down ~14% in a week toward $62k support
items.summary: Bitcoin fell roughly 14% over seven days to the $62,000-$63,500 area, breaking below its 200-week moving average for the first time in this cycle -- a long-horizon technical level that has historically flagged periods of extreme market weakness. The decline tracks the same hawkish Fed repricing and dollar strength hitting gold and miners, compounded by continued spot-ETF outflows exceeding $1bn for a second straight week.
items.actionable: Confirms crypto is trading as a high-beta, rate-sensitive risk asset right now rather than an idiosyncratic story -- its synchronized breakdown with gold/miners reinforces that Fed repricing, not a crypto-specific shock, is the dominant cross-asset driver, useful context for how correlated the precious-metals book may behave if hike odds firm further.

items.headline: Tencent Q3: revenue +8% to RMB207.3bn, but profit -6% as AI capex surges 257%
items.summary: Tencent's Q3 revenue rose 8% YoY to RMB207.3bn with gross profit +7%, but non-IFRS operating and net profit both fell 6% as operating capex payments jumped 257% YoY to RMB63.6bn, pushing free cash flow negative (-RMB69.1bn); excluding new AI products, operating profit was actually up 8%. The stock closed down 0.85% on the print, with WorkBuddy AI assistant surpassing 10 million daily active users and cloud revenue accelerating 35% YoY.
items.actionable: The profit miss is self-inflicted AI-capex spending, not demand weakness (ex-AI operating profit still grew 8%), so the modest -0.85% reaction looks like a justified de-rating of near-term margins rather than a thesis-breaker for the HK-tech sleeve.

items.headline: HSI closes down for HK tech, but Southbound money keeps buying SMIC and Hua Hong -- domestic-chip rotation intact
items.summary: The Hang Seng Index closed lower with tech shares under pressure broadly (Tencent -0.85%, Xiaomi -0.13%), but Southbound Stock Connect recorded roughly HK$2.75bn of net buying, with SMIC and Hua Hong Semiconductor continuing to attract inflows even as the wider tech tape fell. This extends the domestic-chip-self-sufficiency rotation first triggered by the mid-November US export-control tightening.
items.actionable: Southbound money is still net-buying the domestic-foundry names specifically rather than HK tech broadly -- a sign the SMIC chip-rotation position is holding up on its own idiosyncratic merits even as the index-level HK-tech beta stays weak.

items.headline: STI falls for a third straight session on AI-spending caution and US chip-export-curb overhang, despite Nvidia's beat
items.summary: Singapore's Straits Times Index fell to around 5,054.89 (-1.1%) as investor caution over AI capex and lingering US chip-export restrictions outweighed Nvidia's strong Q3 beat and guidance. ST Engineering fell over 2% despite announcing an OCBC-partnered quantum-readiness pilot under the GFTN's Q-FINEX testbed, while Riverstone dropped over 4% on a CEO transition announcement.
items.actionable: The STI's weakness is driven by regional AI-capex/chip-curb sentiment rather than a Singapore-specific shock -- no direct read-through has been flagged yet for the core SGX bank/REIT/developer holdings beyond general risk-off beta.

items.headline: Is the Great Singapore REIT Comeback finally here? SORA easing widens the yield-spread case even as S-REITs lag the STI
items.summary: Analysts flagged early signs of institutional investors returning to S-REITs this week as 3-month compounded SORA continues easing from its 2024 peak, lowering financing costs and widening the distribution-yield spread over risk-free SGS bonds/fixed deposits. The CSOP iEdge S-REIT Leaders Index ETF (SGX: SRT) is still down ~11% YTD as of Nov 5 versus a ~13.7% gain for the broader STI, so the sector remains a laggard even as the rate backdrop improves.
items.actionable: This is a genuine tailwind for the SGX REIT sleeve that is independent of -- and currently diverging from -- the Fed-driven hawkish/dollar-strength narrative hitting precious metals, since Singapore's SORA cycle is easing while the US Fed is still hiking; don't extrapolate the global hawkish-Fed story onto local REIT financing costs.
